title: Jon Stewart’s ‘Daily Show’ Skips David Ellison-Skydance News to Take on AI
description: On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years wh
body:
On Sunday night, John Oliver dedicated the majority of his Emmy-winning show “Last Week Tonight” to the Secret Service’s failings in recent years while declining to address the major media news of the week: David Ellison’s newly-formed Skydance Corp. swallowing up Warner Bros. Discovery — which controls Oliver’s network HBO — and merging it with Paramount Skydance to form a mega-company.

	So, would his late-night compatriot Jon Stewart give his two cents on the merger during Mondays’ episode of “The Daily Show,” since it’s also a part of Skydance Corp.?
	

	Apparently not.

	Stewart dedicated the show entirely to AI, first ripping apart AI leaders’ empty promises of job creation, economic prosperity and its ability to cure cancer while admitting that there’s a 10-25% chance it will kill us all. Currently, however, AI is primarily being used for ICE and other surveillance, drone warfare targeting and potential dynamic pricing at places like McDonald’s.

	“What are we getting in exchange for this 10-25% chance at extinction?” asked Stewart, adding, “Right now it’s mostly murder, surveillance and surge pricing for the McRib? What a trade! I’m getting the sense that you guys might be full of shit.”

	The comedian also pushed back at President Trump allowing these AI companies to self-regulate after his recent fawning AI summit, since the Zuckerberg’s and Musk’s of the world don’t exactly have a sterling track record when it comes to playing it safe. There’s also the matter of how many jobs AI will eliminate. Though AI leaders keep repeating over and over that the technology will lead to newer, different jobs and an economic windfall for everybody, they can’t say what jobs it would create or how it will economically benefit everyday people.
	

	“The view of our self-policing geniuses is that the new world that we are building must continue without regulation or financial limitation because it’s important work carried out by important people,” offered Stewart. “And my guess is: They’ll still have jobs when this is done… Stop lying to us! Claims of universal high income and incredible hobbies isn’t going to paper over how frightening this future can sound.”

schema.headline: Jon Stewart’s ‘Daily Show’ Skips David Ellison-Skydance News to Take on AI

title: Skydance to Fully Reorganize International; Kevin MacLellan Will Not Lead Key Group
description:
Reverberations from the historic combination of Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery are now being felt overseas.

	Despite a Monday report claiming
body:
Reverberations from the historic combination of Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery are now being felt overseas.

	Despite a Monday report claiming international executive Kevin MacLellan was close to clinching the top job outside North America, sources tell Variety he will not move forward in the role.

	While insiders praised him as a transformative leader, the source said David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are looking to thoroughly reorganize the international piece of the newly formed organization. Further information on the international leadership team is not yet available, as the transaction is set to close on Tuesday and operational fallout will continue well into the months ahead.
	

	MacLellan currently serves as Paramount’s president of international and global content distribution, a role he assumed in 2025. Before that, he served as president of international television at NBCUniversal from 2011 to 2013, then as the company’s chairman of global distribution and international from 2013 to 2020.


	In the memo announcing MacLellan’s departure from NBCUniversal in 2019, former Paramount Skydance president Jeff Shell praised him as a “trusted friend and advisor,” noting he oversaw a staff of 2,600 employees in 36 countries and advised on the acquisition of Sky.

	Earlier on Monday, Variety reported that Gerhard Zeiler, president of international for Warner Bros. Discovery, is likely to leave the company ahead of the merger with Paramount after announcing his intention to enter Austrian politics, saying he would bid for leadership of Austria’s ruling Social Democratic Party.
	

	The news follows Ellison’s announcement of the senior executives who will run the newly formed Skydance Corp. on the eve of officially closing the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. 

	Ellison said in a statement, “I’m incredibly proud to introduce the team that will lead Skydance forward, a group that reflects the ambition behind this historic combination. Together, Paramount and Warner Bros. will form a creative-first home with the scale, imagination and technology to define entertainment for a generation.”

	Kreiz commented: “Our goals as a team are to establish Skydance as the premier Hollywood content engine and home for the world’s leading storytellers, accelerate our integrated DTC platform with the best content, leading-edge technology and superior consumer experience, and optimize our highly profitable linear TV portfolio, reaching audiences globally across every entertainment vertical.”

	Casey Bloys, Dana Goldberg, Josh Greenstein, James Gunn, Peter Safran, George Cheeks and JB Perrette are among those set to continue their roles. As previously reported, Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca will not join the new company.

title: Casey Bloys Signs New Multiyear Deal to Continue Overseeing HBO Max and Paramount+ As He Assumes His New Role at Skydance
description: Having just been named to the hefty position of co-chair and chief content officer for Skydance DTC — overseeing both HBO Max and Paramount+, Casey
body:
Having just been named to the hefty position of co-chair and chief content officer for Skydance DTC — overseeing both HBO Max and Paramount+, Casey Bloys is staying put. Variety has confirmed that Bloys — whose contract with HBO was set to expire next year — has signed on for a new multiyear extension.

	Insiders say the new deal for Bloys comes as the exec wants to demonstrate his commitment to the new structure he’s about to run at Skydance, and vice versa. News of Bloys’ new deal came the same day that the new Skydance unveiled its corporate structure.
	

	In announcing Bloys’ expanded role overseeing HBO Max and Paramount+, Skydance noted that included “original programming as well as strategy, operations, communications and performance across the company’s streaming platforms.”


	Bloys had most recently signed a five-year deal in October 2022 than kept him with the company through most of 2027. Terms of his new deal were not revealed, only that it was a “multiyear” pact.

	Besides Bloys, on the television front Skydance confirmed that JB Perrette (previously Warner Bros. Discovery’s CEO and president of global streaming and games) would serve as co-chair and chief business officer of both Skydance TV and Skydance DTC, while George Cheeks (previously chair of TV media at Paramount Skydance) would serve as co-chair and chief content officer, Skydance TV.

	News that Bloys (who previously served as CEO and chief content officer of HBO and HBO Max) would add Paramount+ to his stripes came last week after Paramount direct-to-consumer chair Cindy Holland told colleagues Tuesday that she would be leaving.
	

	Meanwhile, more of the new structure under Bloys should be announced on Tuesday, as Skydance said it would reveal its new executive leadership team “will be issued soon after close.”

	Bloys first joined HBO in 2004 and eventually became exec VP of HBO programming; he became president of HBO programming in 2016 and later added HBO Max to his oversight. Under his watch, HBO and HBO Max series have included “The Pitt,” “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,” “The White Lotus,” “The Last of Us,” “House of the Dragon,” “DTF St. Louis,” “The Penguin,” “Succession,” “Chernobyl,” “Barry,” “Girls,” “Veep,” “Insecure,” “Mare of Easttown” and “Big Little Lies,” with “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” among shows in the pipeline.

	The Ankler was first to report Bloys’ deal renewal.

schema.headline: Casey Bloys Signs New Multiyear Deal to Continue Overseeing HBO Max and Paramount+ As He Assumes His New Role at Skydance

title: Blippi’s Meekah and Dove Release Music Video to Promote Children’s Body Confidence (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Meekah, best friend of children’s entertainment and education character Blippi, has teamed up with Dove on a new music video promoting body confiden
body:
Meekah, best friend of children’s entertainment and education character Blippi, has teamed up with Dove on a new music video promoting body confidence.

	Moonbug Entertainment and the Dove Self-Esteem Project (DSEP) have partnered with Meekah for “My Body Is Amazing,” a music video celebrating movement, self-expression and the amazing things our bodies can do. Designed to protect body confidence from an early age, the music video encourages children to focus on everything their bodies help them experience, explore and enjoy, rather than how they look.
	

	Premiering ahead of International Day of the Girl, the video builds on Moonbug and Dove’s partnership in 2024, when the two brands joined forces on a collection of Blippi episodes and music videos focused on body confidence and self-esteem, including the Blippi “Wonderful Talent Show” special. This time, the partnership brings Meekah’s signature energy, creativity and love of movement to a song all about celebrating the incredible ways our bodies help us experience and explore the world.


	“Meekah is all about encouraging kids to jump in, try something new and find their own way to experience the world,” said Liz Katz, associate general manager of Blippi who leads the Meekah franchise at Moonbug Entertainment. “Movement and self-expression are such a natural part of who she is, and this partnership with Dove gives us a wonderful opportunity to celebrate that. We want kids to feel excited to move, try things, express themselves and, most importantly, have fun being exactly who they are.”

	Dove chief growth marketing officer Marcela Melero said, “For more than 20 years, the Dove Self-Esteem Project has been helping young people build body confidence and self-esteem. And we know that work needs to start early. If we want to reach more children, we need to take body confidence education beyond the classroom and into the things they love to watch and listen to. ‘My Body Is Amazing’ with Meekah does exactly that, celebrating bodies for everything they can do, not simply how they look.”
	

	The Blippi brand averages more than one billion monthly YouTube views and reaches more than 100 million fans worldwide, with Meekah related content averaging more than 200 million monthly YouTube views. Available in 25+ languages, including ASL, across 65+ distribution platforms, the franchise spans streaming, live experiences, products, music, publishing and gaming.

	“My Body Is Amazing can be seen below and is also available on YouTube.

title: Andrew Garfield Says OpenAI’s Sam Altman Seemed ‘F—ing Great’ Before Playing Him in ‘Artificial’: And Then You Learn More About a Person’
description: Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new
body:
Andrew Garfield admits he was initially charmed by Sam Altman before he portrayed the controversial CEO of OpenAI in director Luca Guadagnino’s new film “Artificial.”

	“I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when,” Garfield said on Monday night at the movie’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. “I was like, ‘This guy seems fucking great. He’s honest. He’s transparent. He’s talking about regulation, and he has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control. He’s incredibly charming and charismatic.’ And then you learn more about a person.”
	

	Garfield, who spent “two to three months” listening and watching footage of Altman while preparing to play him, described feeling a moral responsibility to participate in a movie like “Artificial.” When they were filming, Garfield recalls, “there were news stories coming out every day” about the dangers of AI.


	“I wish we could give it even more teeth in a way,” Garfield said. “We need to shine the light as bright as possible at the nooks and crannies of people we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to.”

	Garfield was joined at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall by Guadagnino, writer Simon Rich and actors Yura Borisov (as OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever), Ike Barinholtz (as Elon Musk) and Cooper Hoffman (as OpenAI president Greg Brockman). Monica Barbaro, who portrays OpenAI’s chief technology officer Mira Murati, wasn’t in attendance. The movie charts the evolution of OpenAI and dramatizes the tumultuous time when Altman was controversially fired and then rehired by the AI giant.
	

	Garfield has portrayed many real people on screen, including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” and composer Jonathan Larson in “Tick, Tick… Boom.” It’s a responsibility the actor doesn’t take lightly. 

	“I feel a tremendous amount of compassion for what that must feel like, being on the inside of his soul, going like, ‘That’s not me,’” Garfield said of Altman. “I imagine it would feel confronting. I would feel that way. I’m projecting.”

	In any case, the real Altman seems to be shrugging off “Artificial,” which he hasn’t seen. “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” Altman said in a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, adding that “it will not be good as an accurate depiction.”

	Borisov, a recent Oscar nominee for “Anora,” admits he’s worried about what the real-life Sutskever — and the public — will think about the film.

	“I can’t answer so beautiful like Andrew. That’s why he’s playing Sam,” Borisov joked. “I was nervous to watch this. It was our first time. [I have] so much feeling now about this. It’s like a child just being born, and you’re waiting for it to start breathing.”

	Barinholtz, meanwhile, doesn’t seem too concerned about Musk’s reaction.

	“When you’re playing as someone universally beloved as Elon, and who everyone admires and who is a good person and walks normally…,” Barinholtz cracked. “When I first met with Luca, I said, ‘I have very complicated opinions on Elon.’ And Luca said, ‘It’s not about what you feel about Elon. It’s about finding what he loves about himself.’

	Barinholtz found it “interesting” to play Musk at that particular moment in time. “It’s not at the RNC with the chainsaw. This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, ‘This guy is amazing. He’s going to save you.'”

	Rich, a humorist who worked at “Saturday Night Live” and penned the 2020 satire “An American Pickle,” was inadvertently motivated to write “Artificial” by his childhood friend, Danny Selsam.

	“He started warning me about artificial intelligence in 2008. My friends and I were so shocked by his predictions that we actually discussed potentially doing an intervention to get him medicated, or perhaps institutionalized. We thought he lost his mind,” Rich said. “We took him a little bit more seriously when he joined this new nonprofit called OpenAI.”
	

	A year before ChatGPT was released by OpenAI, Rich says, “Danny started showing us stuff on his computer that was so terrifying that I felt the urge to warn people. When I told journalists what I had seen, they thought it was a hoax. They thought I was trying to prank them.”

	Rich tried to vocalize his concerns, writing about the dangers in columns for outlets like Time magazine. But the public failed to take notice.

	“I quickly realized there’s a limit to what I can do being a non-celebrity and not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Rich said. “So this is kind of a last-ditch effort to warn mankind. I wrote this movie, andI hope to God that a couple people pay attention.”

	A late addition to the NYFF lineup, “Artificial” became one of the year’s buzziest releases after Amazon MGM dropped the nearly completed film, saying the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio.” That’s after Amazon signed a major $50 billion partnership with OpenAI. And Altman is close with Amazon chief Jeff Bezos, having attended his Venetian wedding to Lauren Sanchez in 2025.

	Neon ultimately acquired “Artificial” and plans to release the film in theaters on Dec. 25.

	Landing the world premiere of “Artificial” was a coup for NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim, who described the movie’s festival plans as a “genuinely up-in-the-air situation.” Lim noted that Guadagnino has a long history with New York Film Festival, having premiered movies such as “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt” at prior editions.

	“I thought we would be a great launchpad for the film,” Lim told Variety prior to the premiere. “This is a film that deals with a very pressing situation. AI is in the news practically daily. The film recaps this trajectory that we’ve been on with alarming clarity. And it does this in the form of an incredibly entertaining movie. It has a very dark humor, which is certainly one valid way of approaching the dystopian present.”

schema.headline: Andrew Garfield Says OpenAI’s Sam Altman Seemed ‘F—ing Great’ Before Playing Him in ‘Artificial’: And Then You Learn More About a Person’

title: Trump Says He’ll Pay for ‘Patriotic Ads’ Himself Following Controversy Around Taxpayer-Funded TV Spots
description: After controversy erupted over Donald Trump‘s administration buying TV ad time (with taxpayer dollars) to air advertisements endorsing the president
body:
After controversy erupted over Donald Trump‘s administration buying TV ad time (with taxpayer dollars) to air advertisements endorsing the president, Trump has now said he will fund what he calls “patriotic ads” himself.

	In a statement posted to Truth Social on Monday, Trump wrote: “The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP”
	

	Variety previously reported Thursday that the administration had begun running the advertisements, which say that the president is fighting “communism, socialism and Marxism” as well as “the fake news media” among other claims, on Fox News, Newsmax, CBS, Fox, NBC, MS NOW, CNN and ABC.


	In a statement to Variety, a White House spokesperson said, “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”

	Last month, it was reported that the White House had spent more than $440,000 of U.S. taxpayer dollars on pro-Trump TV ads, which the White House again defended, noting that the “announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” they said, framing the advertisements as an act of patriotism. “Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad. That’s not partisanship — that’s a government that still believes in the country it serves.”

schema.headline: Trump Says He’ll Pay for ‘Patriotic Ads’ Himself Following Controversy Around Taxpayer-Funded TV Spots

title: Fox News Marks 30 Years On Air: ‘We Saw an Opportunity Nobody Else Saw’
description:
Today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast takes a long look back at 30 years since the launch of Fox News Channel. 

	Love it or hate
body:
Today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast takes a long look back at 30 years since the launch of Fox News Channel. 

	Love it or hate it, Fox News has been an influential force in media and politics in the U.S. since its debut on Oct. 7, 1996. 

	Jason Klarman, chief digital officer for Fox News Media, who was part of the channel’s launch marketing team way back in the early Clinton era, discusses the milestone anniversary and the era of media in which Fox News Channel was born. 
	

	Klarman expands on how the Fox News brand built on Fox’s historical “challenger” mentality in the marketplace to eventually rise like a Phoenix to become the TV powerhouse and cultural influencer that it is today. The executive, who was named chief digital officer in 2023, details Fox News’ push over the past decade to try to expand the brand to younger audiences via the Fox Nation streaming platform and a big new podcast slate, among other efforts. 


	Klarman addresses the issue of Fox News evolving into a polarizing brand in the U.S. at a time of heightened partisan tensions in the body politic and ever-increasing fragmentation in TV viewing. He weighs in on how Fox is embracing the world of TikTok and other social media platforms in the quest to stay relevant and create a funnel for future viewers.

	“There is a consistency to Fox that hasn’t changed from 1996 to 30 years later,” Klarman says. “A lot of channels that chased audiences and moved away from what was core to their brand and their ethos — Fox has never done that.”



	

					Jason Klarman, chief digital officer for Fox News Media
	



	Klarman remembers the channel’s humble beginnings, when it launched on just 10 million subscribers on John Malone’s Tele-Communications Inc. systems. 
	

	“It was a slow burn. We used to joke that we were fourth in a three-horse race. We were scrappy. And we did a lot of fun things to bring attention to ourselves,” Klarman says. 

	“I remember when we launched in Atlanta, we went down there, I took the two billboards opposite CNN, and I hired a high school marching band. We unveiled the billboards when we launched on Cox [cable system] in Atlanta.” 

	In the early years, there were a few explosive moments in culture that helped create what would become the Fox News demo were, in Klarman’s view.

	“There were points along the way that we just started to see, incrementally, the distinction between us and the other news organizations. It really began to crystallize. One of those moments was certainly around Monica Lewinsky and the coverage of that. And then the election of 2000 — that was a big one. I think it was an accelerant for us. It was a very hard-fought race right down to the wire,” Klarman says. “And ultimately, it really galvanized the need for a channel called Fox News.”

	(Pictured top: Fox News photos circa 1996; original on-air personalities Sean Hannity and Steve Doocy)

	“Strictly Business” is Variety’s podcast featuring conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment. (Please click here to subscribe to our free newsletter.) New episodes can be downloaded at Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, Spotify, SoundCloud and more.

schema.headline: Fox News Marks 30 Years On Air: ‘We Saw an Opportunity Nobody Else Saw’

title: Neon Sets ‘Artificial’ Oscar Campaign With Andrew Garfield in Supporting Actor, Yura Borisov in Lead (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Sixteen years ago, Andrew Garfield played the Facebook co-founder who was pushed out of the company he helped create in “The Social Network” and cam
body:
Sixteen years ago, Andrew Garfield played the Facebook co-founder who was pushed out of the company he helped create in “The Social Network” and came up short in the supporting actor race. Now, he’s playing the CEO pushed out of OpenAI — and who talked his way back in five days later. Different man, different company. Same category, hoping for a different outcome.

	As “Artificial” world premieres at the New York Film Festival, Variety has learned exclusively that the film’s awards campaign will include Garfield competing in the supporting actor category for Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI drama, while Yura Borisov, who plays OpenAI co-founder and former chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, will campaign in lead actor. Oscar winner Mark Rylance, as AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, will join Garfield in the supporting race, while Monica Barbaro, as former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, will vie for supporting actress.
	

	The campaign will extend across all the major categories, including best picture, director and acting, while Simon Rich’s screenplay will compete in original screenplay and every craft department will receive a full campaign.


	For Guadagnino, “Artificial” marks his fifth appearance at NYFF, following “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All,” “Queer” and “After the Hunt,” which opened the festival last year. After Lincoln Center audiences get the first official look at the film, it heads to the BFI London Film Festival.



	

					Andrew Garfield in “Artificial”
									Neon
	



	Garfield is a two-time best actor nominee for the war drama “Hacksaw Ridge” (2016) and the musical biopic “Tick, Tick … Boom!” (2021). While he has been the face of the marketing and plays the most famous name in the story, it’s not unprecedented for a film’s top-billed star to pursue a supporting nomination — as Meryl Streep did for “Into the Woods” and Oscar winner Catherine Zeta-Jones did for “Chicago.”
	

	The film traces decades in the lives of Ilya and Sam Altman (Garfield), two men from completely different worlds who bond over a shared desire to change the world for the better amid the sunny glow of Obama-era tech optimism. They eventually find themselves at odds as the enormous — and increasingly dangerous — capabilities of their technology reveal themselves across the Trump and Biden years, before Altman is ousted. In other words, the audience rides with the man who pulled the trigger, not the one who took the bullet.

	The best actor field is already crowded, with several contenders emerging from NYFF, including Pedro Pascal’s cellist in “Behemoth!”

	Borisov is two years removed from his first Oscar nomination, for his breakthrough performance as the reluctant henchman Igor in Sean Baker’s best picture winner “Anora.”

	The ensemble has Oscar pedigree throughout. Rylance won supporting actor for his turn in Steven Spielberg’s “Bridge of Spies,” while Barbaro is two years removed from her first nom for playing Joan Baez in the Bob Dylan biopic “A Complete Unknown.” The rest of the cast includes Cooper Hoffman as Greg Brockman, Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd, Billie Lourd and Zosia Mamet.

	Behind the camera, Guadagnino has assembled many of his regular collaborators. Marco Costa, an ACE Eddie Award nominee for “Challengers,” returns for his duties while Jessica Ronane, a two-time Artios nominee who has cast Guadagnino’s films since “Queer,” handled casting. Production designer Stefano Baisi, whose credits include “Queer” and “After the Hunt,” builds the world alongside ADG nominee Roberta Federico. J.W. Anderson, the Costume Designers Guild nominee who dressed “Challengers” and “Queer,” returns as well.

	One of the new faces behind the lens is cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed, a Camerimage winner whose credits include Spike Lee’s “Clockers,” Hype Williams’ “Belly” and Beyoncé’s “Lemonade.” Damon Albarn, the Blur frontman and Grammy winner with Gorillaz, composed the original score and wrote the original songs heard in the film. Submission details for which original songs will vie for attention are forthcoming.

	Guadagnino is hoping to make his triumphant return to an Oscar ceremony. “Call Me by Your Name” earned four nominations at the 90th Oscars and won adapted screenplay for James Ivory. Among the producers are Jeffrey Clifford, Jennifer Fox, Guadagnino, David Heyman and Rich. Fox is an Oscar nominee for best picture for “Michael Clayton,” while Guadagnino was nominated for “Call Me by Your Name.” Heyman is a four-time best picture nominee for “Gravity,” “Marriage Story,” “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Barbie.”
	

	Now, Guadagnino, Garfield and company will see if “Artificial” can prompt their Oscar comebacks.

schema.headline: Neon Sets ‘Artificial’ Oscar Campaign With Andrew Garfield in Supporting Actor, Yura Borisov in Lead (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Artificial’ First Reactions: Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI Drama is ‘Provocative,’ ‘Downright Horrifying’ and His ‘Best Film in a Decade’
description: Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” premiered at the New York Film Festival Monday night, and early reviews have members of the film press championing th
body:
Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” premiered at the New York Film Festival Monday night, and early reviews have members of the film press championing the Sam Altman-centered movie as a “provocative,” “visceral corporate drama” and the director’s “best film in a decade.”

	Next Best Picture editor-in-chief and critic Matt Neglia wrote that “Artificial” is “as entertaining as it is terrifying.” “It’s a brilliantly written human story about power, control, ambition, and greed that might be the most urgently relevant film of our time. Andrew Garfield delivers one of his most unsettling and transformative performances as Sam Altman, equally capturing his disarming charm and unnerving malice.” 
	

	He continued: “Yura Borisov is magnificent as the brilliant mind behind OpenAI, wrestling with the moral implications of the creation he has helped unleash upon the world with intelligence and empathy. Damon Albarn’s electronic, atmospheric score perfectly sets the mood for this tech-driven narrative, while Guadagnino’s cinematic flourishes are bountiful, resulting in what may be his funniest and scariest film to date. Provocative, engaging, and downright horrifying, it’s the movie of the moment that we may not even be able to look back on if the vision of the future it presents comes true.” 


	Editor Eric Kohn called the film a “pitch-perfect dark comedy.” “Andrew Garfield walks a fine line between movie monster, buffoonish mogul, and evil genius. A fun/scary ride that embodies the paradox at its center,” he wrote on X. 

	“Guadagnino guts Silicon Valley with his obsessive pulse & a powerful farce in which Andrew Garfield completely shines,” wrote film critic Jairo Jiménez. “A feverish, visceral corporate drama that proves what is truly artificial was never in the machines, but in the boardroom. An essential film.” 
	

	Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote that “Artificial” is “Guadagnino’s best film in a decade” and “Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov soar to new heights. Loved.”

	Set during the tumultuous time when Altman, OpenAI’s CEO (played by Andrew Garfield), was fired and then rehired by the AI giant in 2023, “Artificial” has faced its own challenges getting to theaters; in June, Neon closed a deal to complete the $40 million film after Amazon MGM Studios dropped the project months earlier after the company signed a major partnership with OpenAI, including a $50 billion investment.

	Despite how hot-button some may feel the film is, Guadagnino told Vulture that he wasn’t “afraid” of Altman’s — or anyone depicted in the film’s — response. “I think that people that have a lot of power should be very much aware that you must be responsible for the community.”

	And though Altman never met Garfield, the tech CEO admitted in a recent Vanity Fair cover story that the actor “did walk like me” when he ran into production filming near his house. “One morning, I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” Altman told Vanity Fair. “It was very strange.”

	“Artificial” reunited Guadagnino with Garfield, who last worked with the director in 2025’s “After the Hunt.” Ike Barinholtz stars as co-founder Elon Musk, Monica Barbaro plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, “Anora” breakout Yura Borisov is former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and Mark Rylance plays Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton. Jason Schwartzman, Zosia Mamet, Cooper Hoffman, Chris O’Dowd, Cooper Koch and Billie Lourd also appear in the film. “SNL” alum Simon Rich penned the script.

	Ahead of the premiere’s conclusion, Variety exclusively reported that Neon’s awards campaign for the film will include Garfield and Rylance competing in the supporting actor category and Borisov campaigning in lead actor. Barbaro will vie for supporting actress.

	“Artificial” opens in theaters on Christmas Day from Neon. Check out first reactions in the posts below.

title: ‘Artificial’ Review: Luca Gaudagnino Has Made the Real Sequel to ‘The Social Network’ — a Brain-Spinning Tech-Geek Docudrama, Brilliantly Acted by Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov
description: Moviegoers will be thrilled to hear that the 2026 fall movie season brings with it a fantastic sequel to “The Social Network.” But I’m not talking a
body:
Moviegoers will be thrilled to hear that the 2026 fall movie season brings with it a fantastic sequel to “The Social Network.” But I’m not talking about “The Social Reckoning” — Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network” (out this Friday), which continues the saga of Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg by hanging the yoke of blame on him for everything that’s wrong with social media. No the real sequel to “The Social Network” is “Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s sprawling, enthralling, brain-spinning drama about the creation of artificial intelligence. (It had its world premiere tonight at the New York Film Festival.)
	

	“Artificial” is a brilliant but playful docudrama, meticulously true to history, that focuses on the founders of OpenAI, notably its CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). But the tale it tells is much larger than that. “Artificial” goes back to the earliest days of AI and shows you how the technology was invented, how it was developed, how it was dreamed. That turns out to be a story unlike any other, because the very nature of artificial intelligence — technology that’s as intelligent and searching as the human mind, or maybe smarter — is that even the people who invented it don’t quite know what it is or what it will do. They have an idea of its potential, but they can’t predict it — they can only let it loose and see what it’s capable of, which will probably be more than anyone bargained for. And by then, it will be impossible to put the genie back in the bottle.


	“Artificial” is about how humanity invented a genie, and maybe a very dark one. Like “The Social Network,” the film shows us a digital “aha” moment that takes on an unexpected life of its own, though in this case two things about the technology are clear from the start: It will change the way we live, and it’s therefore worth a zillion trillion dollars. So this is a dawn-of-a-new-world story, as well as a backstabbing corporate business story, and a horror movie too, in which AI emerges from the lab as a sinister serpent, and the dramatic question is: Who’s going to control it, and how? Most of all, “Artificial” is a human story that shows us what it looks like when people are suddenly in charge of a force they devised that may be more powerful than they are.
	

	It’s been a long time since I saw a film that attained this next-level feeling of topical charge. A lot of people will go into “Artificial,” as I did, not knowing all that much about AI and feeling as if it’s a frosty and abstract frontier. Yet as you watch the film, AI comes alive as a subject. It becomes real — you touch what it is, what it means, what the stakes are. The result is a movie that’s at once inspiring and deeply chilling, and when it’s over you’re in a different place. And that is what a ripped-from-the-headlines movie should do. It shouldn’t merely be a dramatization of what we already know but, rather, a future-shock referendum on our lives and our values and maybe our souls. “Artificial” does that thing.

	The screenplay, by Simon Rich, is pitched at a high-wire level of tech-geek patter, to the point that you may not follow every line. Yet that’s part of the film’s exhilaration — it keeps you on the edge of your brain — and it’s also what gives it the ring of authenticity. This is exactly how these dudes think, and how they talk. (Most of them are dudes, though not all.) The film opens in Toronto in 2003, where Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov), a 17-year-old graduate of the University of Toronto, walks into the classroom of Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), a British-Canadian computer scientist who’s been trying to work up a model of artificial intelligence. Ilya is looking for work as an assistant, and the professor, with his dandyish nerd arrogance, tells him to look at a paper he’s written and come back in a few days. Minutes later, Ilya returns, having looked deeper into the material than the professor has, and he’s scrawling an equation on the blackboard that Hinton says “took him five years to learn.”

	Ilya, you see, is a stone-cold genius. He’s like the Einstein of AI, with an ability to see models of it rotating in his head. He’s also a Russian émigré who speaks in an accent as thick as borscht and gazes out at the world with a stunted glower of beetle-browed sincerity that makes it look like it’s never occurred to him in this life to tell a joke or even to laugh. This is a personality of complete tech-geek maximalism. Yet playing this driven, earnest, possibly on-the-spectrum visionary of the computer age, Yora Borisov, the bald co-star of “Anora” (he sports short dark hair here, gathered in unkempt tufts and clumps), gives what may be the performance of the year. His Ilya can seem hard to warm up to at first, but he’s an authentic human being, who we begin to form an attachment to, especially when he starts to warn about the dangers of AI. What draws us to him is that he’s the key inventor of the brave new world, and also the only one who fully gets it. And Borisov shades that with grace notes of tragedy. 
	

	By 2012, Ilya and Hinton have comes up with an AI model that’s developed enough to place in an auction. Within five seconds, there’s a bid on the table for $20 million. Ilya and Hinton decide to sell their knowledge to Google. They will set up a lab there, working independently, and have their research funded. This works for a while, but John (Chris O’Dowd), the Google executive in charge, doesn’t get where they’re going with AI. He’s not onboard with the vision of it. Sam Altman, a rising star of Silicon Valley, is.

	Gaudagino’s last stab at zeitgeist topicality, “After the Hunt,” turned out to be a mixed bag, but in “Artificial” he’s at the top of his game, working with the impish human factor that was there in “Challengers,” his slyly enthralling tennis-triangle movie. Guadagnino stages the film as an eclectic jamboree of brainstorming sessions and office showdowns and bro parties, and he gives it all a dramatic hotfoot with the scenes that include Elon Musk, played by Ike Barinholtz in an irresistible showbiz turn that lands just this side of caricature. His Elon is the god of the geeks and knows it. Dressed in black, holding his body at skewed “rock star” angles, his mouth turned down into a grimace of power, he’s the one who can make things happen. Guadagnino stages a group dinner, in which Ilya gets to know Altman and his pals (this is where it’s first revealed that Altman is gay), and Musk crashes in like the lord of the frat house. His bluster is easy to mock, but he’s quicker than anyone in the room, and he goes in with Altman on backing OpenAI.

	As it turns out, Elon is too quick for his own good. He wants the AI models advanced, faster and faster, so that they can kill the competition. But with AI it’s not going to work like that. That’s why he opts out, and Altman takes over as sole CEO. There’s a way that the film catches the audience up in the booster spirit of early AI, when everyone is convinced that it’s going to be a powerful force for good. It will solve world hunger, and teach the immune system how to beat cancer cells. The technology will achieve critical mass when it becomes AGI (artificial general intelligence), which means that it’s now teaching itself how to think. This first happens when AI plays — and wins — a video game with one of the OpenAI geeks, and the super-slow-motion beer-spraying party scene that follows is bravura filmmaking, expressing how the lust for computers to take over our world has become nearly sexual.
	

	At OpenAI, the dude slogan, led by Ilya, is “Feel the AGI,” which is a kind of Peter Pan mantra. It means: The technology will come to life — literally — if you believe in it. But the moment where Ilya learns that AI has become so smart that it can tell a joke, and lie…at that point, you feel the world shift. The documentary “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist” captured many of the same issues, but to see the monster actually rise up before your eyes, to the point that its creators are terrified, gives “Artificial” an ominous power.

	The movie takes us deep into the tech world, and its ultimate paradox: the way that our tech reality, which can seem so coldly factual, is actually shaped by personality. The performances sizzle, from Cooper Hoffman’s Adam Sandler-on-Adderall turn as the OpenAI super-geek Greg Brockman to Monica Barbaro as the ambiguously tranquil Mira Murati, who becomes the company’s chief technology officer, to Rylance’s delectable professor to Jason Schwartzman as ex-academic hippie who has foreseen all the dangers of AI. The conversation he has on a San Francisco bench with Yuri is the movie’s equivalent of Donald Sutherland’s great scene in “JFK,” and it leaves a chill hanging in the air.

	And then there is Sam Altman. Garfield plays him as a corporate seducer, and he does it by seducing the audience, making Altman winsome in his enthusiasm, a softly charismatic player who believes in the right things. And he really does…until he doesn’t. The central conflict in “Artificial” is this: The development of technology moves so quickly that for your company to succeed, to thrive, or simply to survive, you’ve got to win. You’ve got to be first. And that puts the emphasis on speed. But Ilya, cognizant of the profound dangers of AI, says that the new technology must be developed in tandem with an appreciation for how threatening it is. The trick is that it has to be developed through interaction with humanity…because it literally evolves by doing that. So…easy does it. Test it all out.

	But that doesn’t chime with the business plan. As the film goes on, Garfield’s performance grows more layered and duplicitous in a nearly subliminal way, as we start to pick up on the priorities lurking just beneath Sam’s silky manners. He wants to advance the tech — which is what tech bros are supposed to do. But AI isn’t like other tech. Throwing safety to the winds could be throwing civilization into the trash.
	

	Is that what’s happening now? The power of “Artificial” is that it so ominously captures the ambiguous place we’re now in with AI — on the cusp of a revolution, with warnings in place, yet no one is there to regulate it. (Obviously, that should be the U.S. government, but under the current leader we barely have one.) Garfield’s Altman becomes the seducer-as-betrayer, but the film is about something much bigger than his being the “bad guy.” In “Artificial,” everyone goes along with Altman, even after he’s fired from OpenAI, because he convinces them that if they don’t go along with him, the only other options are worse. The film is about the victory of greed, but it’s also about something as sinister as “Invasion of the Body Snatchers.” What’s been snatched away is our desire to guide our own destiny, and maybe even to be who we are. At the end of “Artificial,” we’ve handed that away all too eagerly, ceding our power to the ghost in the machine.

description:
'Ghost Adventures' Zak Bagans
                          Buys Vegas Bunker for $4.5M ... Plans to
body:
'Ghost Adventures' Zak Bagans
                          Buys Vegas Bunker for $4.5M ... Plans to Make it a Museum!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 5, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            It sounds like Zak Bagans has another ghost adventure brewing ... this time in the Vegas bunker house he just bought, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The "Ghost Adventures" star dropped $4.5 mil on the 16,000-square-foot property, which boasts painted skies, fake landscaping, a pool, and lighting designed to replicate the different hours of the day -- the sprawling home is known as the "Underground Mansion" and has a Cold War luxury bunker hidden nearly three stories beneath an ordinary home.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Apparently, when Zak did a walk-through of the impressive estate, he learned about the bunker's dark history, which was so spooky that some staff refused to go down there alone.
      
    
            MrBeast filmed there and called it “one of the most expensive and bizarre bunkers on the planet,” and Imagine Dragons shot the video for “Monday” inside the bunker.
      
    
            TMZ has learned that Bagans plans to make it into a museum, opening it to the public for the first time. We're told he also wants to make an original documentary feature.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He says ... "Once I was actually in the process of buying it, I was shocked by how many different mysteries are tied to this house, things I don’t wanna reveal just yet."
      
    
            Zak says he plans to preserve the house and its history, so he can "dig deeper into the mysteries."
      
    
            Holly Erker of IS Luxury held the listing and Rob Jensen with Rob Jensen Company represented Zak.

title: Televangelist Jim Bakker Dies at 86
body:
Televangelist Jim Bakker
                          Dead at 86
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 5, 2026
                            7:22 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a Christian television empire with his former wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, has died.
      
    
            His wife, Lori Bakker, announced Jim died Monday evening saying he devoted 66 years to preaching the Gospel and remained committed to his ministry until the end.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            Lori described him as her husband and best friend, adding that his heart remained with the ministry and its supporters during his final days. She asked for prayers and privacy as the family grieves.
      
    
            His cause of death is currently not yet known.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Bakker rose to prominence in the 1970s as co-host of "The PTL Club," which he launched with Tammy Faye. The pair also founded Heritage USA, a Christian theme park in South Carolina.
      
    
            Their empire collapsed in the late 1980s amid a sex and money scandal. Bakker was convicted of fraud and conspiracy after misusing ministry funds and selling "lifetime memberships" to a hotel that was never completed. He was sentenced to 45 years in prison, though he ultimately served about five years.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After his release, Bakker returned to television and later launched "The Jim Bakker Show" with Lori, where he discussed Christianity, biblical prophecy and current events.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tammy Faye divorced Jim while he was incarcerated and later married Roe Messner. She died of cancer in 2007. Jim and Tammy Faye shared two children, including their son, Jay Bakker.
      
    
            Jim was 86.
      
    
            RIP.

title: Cornell Frat Bro’s Lawyer Slams University Officials In Private Emails: 'Shame On You All'
description:
Cornell Frat Bro's Lawyer
                          Goes After University Officials in Private Emails
body:
Cornell Frat Bro's Lawyer
                          Goes After University Officials in Private Emails
                          'Shame On You All'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 5, 2026
                            6:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A lawyer for one of the Cornell fraternity brothers being sued over the alleged gang rape blasted the university during the investigation back in 2025 ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained an alleged email, dated May 16, 2025, from an attorney named Jeremy Saland -- who represented one of the accused men -- to Cornell officials as part of the Title IX probe.
      
    
            In the letter, Jeremy claimed one of the panel members who decided the consequences for his client was distracted and driving during one witness’ testimony. He said he asked for the hearing to be adjourned for the day, but his request was denied.
      

            Saland stated, “No matter who ultimately made the decision, and no matter how willful Cornell’s continued disregard for the rule of law, honesty, integrity, and any ethical consideration to an accused – especially in light of the demonstrable evidence or lack of evidence confirming [redacted] innocence, aka, non-responsibility, it is incredibly galling and frightening.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He added, “I cannot help but wonder whether this misconduct and disregard is common at your esteemed and respected Ivy League institution and whether the same warrants greater investigation."
      
    
            In another alleged email from a few days later, Jeremy wrote to officials, “Sadly, for Cornell, whether [redacted] is responsible or not, the esteemed Ivy League university’s failings will not be ignored. No student should be subject to such a lack of professionalism. After all, Cornell should be setting the bar, not lowering it in a sinister game of limbo.”
      
    
            He ended this email by saying, “Whether by the hand or word of President Donald Trump or Cornell University, appearing to do what is right when you know that is not, is always wrong. Do better. Shame on you all.”
      
    
            The school ultimately determined the fraternity brother had committed attempted sexual exploitation. As part of his punishment, Cornell had him take a class on issues of social media and sexual harassment, write a “reflection” paper, and issued a no-contact order with the accuser.
